clinicalPearls: Primary HSV infection produces erythema followed by hallmark painful grouped vesicles that may evolve into pustules and ulcerate, especially on mucosal surfaces; lesions appear at the site of inoculation (Harrison p.~1010, App. A1).
HSV-1 classically causes orolabial disease (cold sores, herpes labialis) and HSV-2 causes genital lesions, but either type can infect either site (Harrison p.1050).
Non-genital cutaneous presentations include herpes gladiatorum (head and neck of young wrestlers) and herpetic whitlow (digits of health care workers) (Harrison p.1050).

Primary acute herpetic gingivostomatitis (usually HSV-1) presents with labial vesicles that rupture and crust plus intraoral vesicles that quickly ulcerate; it is extremely painful, with acute gingivitis, fever, malaise, foul odor, and cervical lymphadenopathy, occurring primarily in infants, children, and young adults (Harrison p.~325, Table 38-1).
Recurrent disease is milder than primary infection, and there is typically no fever in recurrent infection; herpes labialis recurrences typically do not involve the oral mucosa (Harrison App. A1).
Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide, and there is a documented positive-feedback loop between HSV and HIV transmission (Harrison p.1096).
Although the HSV–HIV epidemiologic link is consistent, randomized trials of antiviral suppression of HSV showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison p.1096).
harrison.pathophysiology: HSV-1 and HSV-2 are neurotropic DNA herpesviruses that establish lifelong latency in sensory ganglia after primary mucocutaneous infection; periodic reactivation produces recurrent localized disease (e.g., recurrent herpes labialis with HSV-1 and herpes genitalis with HSV-2). Virus enters and replicates within the epidermis at the site of inoculation. In HSV encephalitis there is characteristic unilateral temporal-lobe involvement. The virus can disseminate, particularly in the setting of disrupted skin (eczema herpeticum) or impaired cell-mediated immunity; visceral dissemination may occur even with only localized mucocutaneous disease (Harrison pp.1050, 1010 App. A1, p.747).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of genital ulcer disease (e.g., syphilis, chancroid) in genital HSV
infectionMimics: Varicella-zoster virus infection (vesicular lesions are individually similar to HSV; Tzanck smear cannot distinguish them)
Reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) due to Mycoplasma/other respiratory infections, which mimics mucositis seen with HSV-associated erythema multiforme
Disseminated VZV versus disseminated HSV (individual lesions similar for VZV and HSV)
nonInfectiousMimics: Erythema multiforme major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (HSV is itself a common trigger of EM, but drug-induced SJS/TEN must be distinguished)
additionalInvestigations: PCR of CSF for HSV in suspected encephalitis (diagnostic test of choice; may be falsely negative early in the course of disease) (Harrison p.747)
Tzanck smear of an early unroofed vesicle (Giemsa/Wright stain): multinucleated epithelial giant cells suggest HSV or VZV, but cannot identify the specific virus (Harrison p.~480)
Viral culture, immunofluorescence microscopy, or genetic/PCR testing to identify the specific virus type (Harrison p.~480)
In FUO with headache, CSF microbiologic examination including HSV (especially type 2) (Harrison p.~149)
redFlags: Fever with decreased level of consciousness and unilateral temporal-lobe involvement on imaging suggests HSV encephalitis - start empiric aciclovir promptly because CSF PCR may be falsely negative early (Harrison p.747)
Disseminated/visceral HSV in immunocompromised or neonatal patients; HSV can disseminate viscerally even with only localized mucocutaneous disease
Eczema herpeticum (HSV dissemination in eczematous skin)
Neonatal HSV disease (skin lesions are diagnostically helpful when present but may be absent)
harrison.prognosis: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis heals spontaneously in 10-14 days; lesions persisting beyond 3 weeks (unless secondarily infected) are not due to primary HSV infection. Recurrent disease is generally milder than primary infection. Approximately 25% of patients with herpes simplex encephalitis subsequently develop an autoimmune (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis weeks after the viral infection resolves - in children often with choreoathetosis and in adults with cognitive/psychiatric symptoms (Harrison pp.325, 821).
pitfalls: CSF HSV PCR may be falsely negative early in the course of encephalitis, so a negative early result does not exclude the diagnosis and should not delay empiric aciclovir (Harrison p.747)
Tzanck smear cannot distinguish HSV from VZV; type-specific identification requires culture, immunofluorescence, or genetic testing (Harrison p.~480)
HSV visceral dissemination can occur with only localized mucocutaneous disease, so absence of widespread skin lesions does not exclude serious systemic infection (Harrison App. A1)
Oral lesions lasting more than 3 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis rather than primary HSV (Harrison Table 38-1)
